summary.text: The small intestine is a long, folded organ of the gastrointestinal tract, between the stomach and large intestine, where most nutrient absorption takes place.
It has three regions: the duodenum, the jejunum, and the ileum.
It is called small because it is narrower than the large intestine, even though it is longer.

facts.label: Typical length
facts.value: 3 to 5 metres in a living person

facts.label: Duodenum shape
facts.value: A short C that surrounds the head of the pancreas

facts.label: Ileum's main job
facts.value: Absorbing vitamin B₁₂ and bile salts

items.prompt: The small intestine is longer than the large intestine. Why is it still called small?

options.label: It holds less food at one time
It is shorter than the stomach
It is narrower in diameter
It is made of fewer sections

items.explain: It is longer than the large intestine but narrower in diameter, which is why it is called small.

items.prompt: Acidic chyme arrives from the stomach into the first section of the small intestine. What neutralizes the acid there?

options.label: Extra hydrochloric acid from the liver
Bicarbonate from glands in the duodenum and from the pancreas
Water drawn in from the large intestine
Bile acting as the only buffer

items.explain: The duodenum's glands make an alkaline mucus with bicarbonate, which together with pancreatic bicarbonate neutralizes the stomach acids.

items.prompt: An organ built to soak up nutrients has a lining with folds, villi, and microvilli. What do these do?

options.label: They enlarge the area available for absorbing
They slow food so it cannot move on
They produce the bile that breaks down fat
They hold the intestine in place in the abdomen

items.explain: Folds, villi, and microvilli enlarge the mucosa's surface to an average of 30 square metres.

items.prompt: The final section of the small intestine specializes in absorbing what?

options.label: The starch breakdown done by amylase
Bicarbonate that neutralizes acid
Bile stored for later release
Vitamin B₁₂ and bile salts

items.explain: The ileum mainly absorbs vitamin B₁₂ and bile salts, plus anything the jejunum did not absorb.

items.prompt: Partly digested food reaches the first section of the small intestine and meets juices from two other organs. Which two?

options.label: The salivary glands and the spleen
The pancreas and the liver
The spleen and the large intestine
The tongue and the stomach glands

items.explain: The duodenum receives gastric chyme together with digestive juices from the pancreas and the liver.

items.prompt: Two measurements of the same person's small intestine differ by a few metres. What could explain this?

options.label: It grows longer after every meal
It shortens as the person ages
It depends on the person's height and how it is measured
It depends only on how much they ate

items.explain: Length varies with height and with measuring method; measurements are longer after death and when the bowel is empty.

paragraphs.heading: Where food is absorbed
paragraphs.text: The small intestine, also called the small bowel, is the part of the gastrointestinal tract where most nutrients from food are absorbed. It runs from the stomach to the large intestine and receives bile and pancreatic juice that help with digestion. It is actually longer than the large intestine; the name comes from it being narrower. Folded many times over to fit in the abdomen, it measures about 6.5 metres.

paragraphs.heading: A length that varies
paragraphs.text: That length is far from fixed. Reported values range from about 3 metres to 10.5 metres, partly depending on how it is measured, and in a living person 3 to 5 metres is typical. Taller people tend to have longer ones, and measurements usually come out longer after death and when the bowel is empty. Its width is about 1.5 centimetres in newborns after 35 weeks of gestation and 2.5 to 3 centimetres in adults.

paragraphs.heading: Three regions
paragraphs.text: It has three parts: the duodenum, the jejunum and the ileum. The duodenum is the shortest, and it is where food starts being readied for absorption through villi, tiny finger-like bumps on the lining. The jejunum takes in small nutrient particles, already digested by enzymes in the duodenum, through lining cells called enterocytes. The ileum takes up vitamin B₁₂, bile salts and whatever the jejunum did not absorb. Folds, villi and microvilli give the lining an average surface area of 30 square metres.

paragraphs.heading: The duodenum
paragraphs.text: The duodenum is a C-shaped section 20 to 25 centimetres long that wraps around the head of the pancreas. It receives gastric chyme, the food arriving from the stomach, along with enzymes from the pancreas and bile from the liver. The enzymes break down proteins, while bile emulsifies fats into micelles. Brunner's glands in the duodenum release an alkaline, mucus-rich fluid with bicarbonate, which, together with bicarbonate from the pancreas, neutralizes the stomach acid in the chyme.

paragraphs.heading: The jejunum and the ileum
paragraphs.text: Next comes the jejunum, the middle section, about 2.5 metres long, which begins at the suspensory muscle of the duodenum. Circular folds and villi increase its surface, and sugars, amino acids and fatty acids pass into the bloodstream here. The ileum, the final section at about 3 metres, has villi like the jejunum and mainly absorbs vitamin B₁₂ and bile acids plus any other leftover nutrients. It joins the cecum, part of the large intestine, at the ileocecal junction.

paragraphs.heading: Held in place and fed with blood
paragraphs.text: The jejunum and ileum hang in the abdomen from the mesentery, a part of the peritoneum through which arteries, veins, lymph vessels and nerves run. Blood reaches the small intestine from the celiac trunk and the superior mesenteric artery, both branches of the aorta. The jejunum and ileum get their blood from the superior mesenteric artery.
